definition: Heat setting stabilizes thermoplastic fibers, yarns or fabrics by heating them above their glass transition temperature in a chosen shape and then cooling, so shape and dimensions persist in later use.
explanation: Thermoplastic fibers such as polyester and nylon carry internal stresses from drawing, texturing, knitting or weaving, which cause shrinkage or distortion when they are later heated. In heat setting the material is held at defined dimensions, for example pinned on a stenter frame for fabric or wound in packages in an autoclave for yarn, and heated with hot air, contact heat or steam. Chain segments gain mobility, stresses relax and the crystalline structure reorganizes; cooling below the glass transition then locks in the new configuration. The same principle sets texturing crimp and permanent pleats.
example: A knitter of polyester and elastane sportswear finds that unset fabric curls at the edges and shrinks unevenly in dyeing. After the greige fabric is pinned on a stenter at its target width and passed through a hot chamber, it lies flat, holds its width through dyeing and keeps its dimensions after home laundering at ordinary temperatures.
caution: Heat setting applies to thermoplastic fibers; cotton, wool and viscose are not heat set in this sense, and wool is set with moisture, heat and chemistry instead. The set holds only below the setting temperature, so ironing or drying hotter than the set point can undo or distort it. Excess temperature can yellow, stiffen or glaze fabric and weaken elastane.
deeper: Setting temperatures must lie above the glass transition temperature (Tg), where amorphous chain segments become mobile, and below the melting point, where the oriented structure would be lost; for PET, Tg is about 75 C. A review of melt-spun fibers describes annealing under strain, or heat setting, as partially relaxing frozen-in stresses from drawing and perfecting and stabilizing the microstructure, so shrinkage on later heating falls. A set is generally stable against later exposures below the highest effective temperature the fiber has experienced. Water plasticizes polyamides and lowers their effective Tg, which helps explain why steam and hot-wet conditions are effective for setting nylon. In false-twist texturing of polyester, heater temperatures around 200 C and above are reported for setting the twisted configuration.
origins: Heat setting became essential once melt-spun synthetics reached textile mills in the mid-twentieth century, beginning with nylon from Wallace Carothers's polymer research at DuPont and followed by polyester. Producers found that these thermoplastic fibers could be given a lasting shape by heat, enabling dimensionally stable knits, durable pleats and textured stretch yarns. It remains a routine step in finishing synthetic wovens and knits and in processing carpet yarns, placed before or after dyeing depending on the fabric.

definition: High-twist describes yarns spun or thrown with more turns than a comparable soft-spun yarn, producing a springy, often drier hand used in crepes, voiles and tropical suitings such as fresco.
explanation: Twist level is meaningful only relative to yarn linear density: the same turns per meter that feel high in a coarse yarn may be ordinary in a fine one, which is why mills use twist factors or multipliers. Raising twist packs fibers more tightly, increases yarn liveliness and can improve crease recovery, but it also reduces bulk and can make cloth wiry if overdone. In wool suiting, high-twist worsted singles or two-folds are a common route to fresco-type tropical fabrics. In dress goods, still higher crepe twists create pebble textures after wet finishing. Always read high-twist beside the fiber, count and fabric sett rather than as a free-standing quality grade.
example: A tailor compares two navy tropical cloths of similar weight. One uses softly twisted yarns and feels smoother but shows sitting creases quickly; the other uses high-twist yarns, feels drier and more granular, and springs back after a commute. The fiber content line on both labels may say only virgin wool. The twist and sett, not a Super number alone, explain most of the difference you feel.
caution: High-twist is not a regulated label and not a substitute for micron, Super S or weave. Excessive twist can hurt tensile efficiency, raise torque and make seams smile if the cloth is not balanced. Marketing that equates high-twist with cooler or more breathable without air-permeability or wearer data is incomplete. Crepe-twist dress fabrics and fresco suitings share the twist idea but are different end products.
deeper: As twist rises, fiber helix angles increase and lateral pressure inside the yarn grows, raising fiber-to-fiber friction until an optimum strength point; beyond that, strength falls because fibers lie too oblique to carry axial load. High twist also reduces yarn diameter slightly for a given count and lowers hairiness, changing light scatter and perceived dryness. In woven cloth, pairing high-twist yarns with an open sett is a classic tropical strategy: the yarn supplies spring, the sett supplies porosity. Crepe fabrics instead rely on twist liveliness plus finishing shrinkage to grain the surface. Specifying turns per meter with count, or quoting a twist multiplier, is the only way to compare high-twist claims across suppliers.
origins: Spinners have long varied twist for strength, sheerness and texture, from voile and crepe traditions to tropical suitings for warm climates. English and continental mills codified high-twist worsted tropicals in the twentieth-century tailoring trade, including trademarked fresco-type cloths. The everyday phrase high-twist later spread through ready-to-wear as a shorthand for dry, resilient summer cloths. The underlying physics of twist multipliers is older still, rooted in spinning engineering rather than in any single brand story.

definition: Jersey, or single jersey, is the basic weft-knitted fabric made on one set of needles, with V-shaped loop legs on the technical face and loop heads on the technical back.
explanation: In weft knitting a single yarn feeds across the width, forming a row of loops (a course) that is pulled through the previous row. Vertical columns of loops are wales. In single jersey all loops are drawn through to the same side, so the technical face shows smooth columns of V shapes and the technical back shows rows of semicircular loop heads. This imbalance makes edges curl and gives the fabric more stretch across the width than along its length.
example: Turn a plain T-shirt inside out and look closely. The outside shows neat vertical V columns; the inside shows horizontal bumps. Cut a strip across the body and it curls toward the face along the cut edges. Pull a snagged yarn and a run can travel down a wale. Measuring courses and wales per centimeter on both samples lets a student compare their knitting density.
caution: Jersey names a structure, not a fiber, and does not imply elastane. Its stretch comes from loop geometry. Jersey knits are prone to curling, laddering, and spirality, where wales skew after washing, often from twist-lively yarn. Double jersey fabrics such as interlock use two needle beds and behave differently. Fabric weight and loop length matter as much as the structure name.
deeper: Key parameters are stitch or loop length, courses and wales per unit length, yarn linear density and tightness factor, commonly the square root of yarn tex divided by loop length. Relaxed dimensions settle toward values governed mainly by loop length, which is why shrinkage control in knits focuses on relaxation and compaction. Single jersey spirality arises when residual yarn torque rotates loops, so ply, twist balance and relaxation treatments are used to reduce it. Studies holding machine settings constant report that both fiber type and structure, comparing plain single jersey with lacoste (pique) variants, influence bursting strength, pilling, abrasion and wicking. Comfort trials also report differences between single jersey and mesh knits in microclimate humidity during exercise.
origins: The fabric name is conventionally associated with the Channel Island of Jersey and its knitted goods; this edition did not verify a dated first use. Mechanized weft knitting later made single jersey a staple of underwear and T-shirt production on circular machines, where it is produced as a tube at high speed. Handknitters know the same structure as stockinette or stocking stitch.
